name: Fits Duo
tagline: A wardrobe app for cataloging clothes and getting outfit pairings.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Under the hood this is a photo library with tags and a pairing rule set, which an agent can scaffold in an afternoon. The genuinely hard parts are not the data model: clean cutouts of garments, a camera flow that does not feel like filing taxes, and suggestions that read as taste rather than color-wheel math. A local build will happily store every shirt you own and produce combinations that are technically valid and visually cursed. If you mostly want a searchable record of what you own and a nudge toward combos you forgot about, the DIY version is fine. If you want the thing to feel good enough that you open it before leaving the house, that is a polish problem, and polish is what you are paying for.
coreLoopDIY: Photograph each garment, auto-cut the background, tag it by slot and color, then generate and save outfit combinations from your own closet.
requirements: A phone or camera for garment photos
Patience for the tagging slog on an existing wardrobe
whatYouLose: Polished mobile capture and cropping that works one-handed in bad bedroom lighting
Suggestion quality that reflects actual styling sense instead of hue arithmetic
Any shared or partner-facing view, if that is the point of the product
Sync across devices, so your closet lives on whatever machine built it
Someone else maintaining the background-removal model when it chokes on black jeans
moatNotes: Wardrobe apps live or die on capture friction. Every one of them is a database wearing a nice coat.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the value is almost entirely in whether you keep using it, and that depends on the five seconds it takes to add a garment and the one second it takes to trust a suggestion. A self-built version gets abandoned at item thirty when the cutouts look bad and the recommendations pair a suit jacket with running shorts. Paying for it means someone already fought that fight, on a phone, with a real camera pipeline.
notes: Easy to build, hard to keep opening. That gap is the whole product.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal wardrobe and outfit app. Stack: Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite via better-sqlite3, images stored on local disk under ./data/images. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics.

Data model:
- garment: id, name, slot (top, bottom, outer, shoes, accessory), colors (array of hex), pattern, season tags, formality 1-5, image path, notes, archived flag
- outfit: id, name, array of garment ids, occasion tag, rating 1-5, created date, last worn date

Features that are IN:
1. Add garment flow: upload or camera capture, run background removal in the browser with @imgly/background-removal, show the cutout, let the user crop and accept or retry.
2. Auto-extract the top 3 dominant colors from the cutout and prefill the color field; the user can edit.
3. Closet grid view with filters by slot, color family, season, and formality.
4. Outfit builder: pick one garment per slot, see them stacked on a neutral canvas, save as an outfit.
5. Suggest button: generate 10 candidate outfits from the closet scored by a transparent rule set (formality within 1 point, no more than one loud pattern, neutral-anchored color pairing, season match). Show the score breakdown so the user can see why.
6. Wear log: mark an outfit worn today, surface least-worn garments.
7. Export everything to a zip of images plus a JSON file. Import the same zip back.

OUT of scope: user accounts, sharing, sync, AI image generation, virtual try-on, any paid API, any shop or affiliate links.

Setup: npm install, npm run db:init to create the SQLite schema, npm run dev. Put nothing secret in code; if any key is ever needed, read it from .env and ship a .env.example. Write a README with the setup steps and one paragraph explaining the suggestion scoring rules in plain language.
